page: Amazon Web Services r8gb.48xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro System and powered by the ARMv9 AWS Graviton Neoverse-V2 architecture. The instance provides 192 dedicated physical cores and 192 vCPUs operating at 2.7 GHz without simultaneous multithreading. It is equipped with 1536.0 GB of system memory, yielding an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware features include 64 KB L1 data cache, 2 MB L2 cache, 36 MB L3 cache, and hardware AES acceleration. There is no bundled local storage, and the instance does not feature discrete GPUs, but it offers a high network baseline speed of 400 Gbps.

Benchmark results highlight massive multi-core throughput and exceptional memory bandwidth. In stress-ng, multi-core CPU performance reaches 314,834.98, placing it in the top 10%, while single-core performance settles in the average tier at 1643.79. Memory bandwidth tests demonstrate top-tier throughput, recording 960.8 GB/sec for uncached read blocks and 483.48 GB/sec for uncached write blocks. Application workloads show extraordinary capability in data handling, with Redis SET operations achieving 359.67 million operations per second, PassMark database operations scoring 47,131.96, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression hitting 1,412.6 GB/sec.

The primary tradeoff of the r8gb.48xlarge lies in single-threaded performance versus parallel capacity. While Geekbench multi-core (19,740.0), Clang compilation (86,839.0), and ray tracing (134,258.0) demonstrate upper-tier parallelism, Geekbench single-core (1656.0) and image processing (2,922.0) reflect moderate or weak per-core execution speeds. Additionally, LLM prompt processing scales unevenly, scoring low for small 135M models (224.06 tokens/sec) but achieving top-25% results on medium 7B models (192.36 tokens/sec). The absence of bundled NVMe storage requires all persistent storage to be attached over the network.

Given its 1.5 TB memory allocation, 400 Gbps network interface, and immense parallel data throughput, the AWS r8gb.48xlarge is well positioned for in-memory databases, large-scale distributed caching, big data analytics, and high-throughput static web serving.
